meta.regime: The regime has narrowed to one variable: energy. For two weeks this book described policy differentials against a weakening dollar, with oil as a side story. Today oil IS the story, and the dollar leg has stopped paying. Crude rose for a third consecutive session to WTI 85.37 and Brent 91.51 - the highest of the conflict - because President Trump said he is not interested in extending the interim peace memorandum that formally lapsed on Monday, because Washington will not back any Iran-Oman corridor arrangement that does not guarantee unrestricted passage, and because only five commodity vessels transited Hormuz on Saturday and NONE on Sunday against 31 the previous weekend. The transmission is now measurable rather than theoretical: Canada's July CPI rebounded to 3.0% from 2.8% with gasoline inflation at 25.7% and every Bank of Canada core measure ticking higher, which is the first hard print anywhere showing the energy shock reaching core. Risk assets are repricing it - Nikkei -2.20%, US100 -1.00%, DE40 -0.37%, ASX200 -0.39% - and, importantly, the metals did NOT act as havens: gold fell 0.68% to 4,386, silver 1.41% to 64.84 and copper 0.72% to 6.56 in a single broad retreat. The dollar index is 99.65 and HIGHER, having stopped making lows for the first time in a week, with the US 10-year at 4.744% and NY Empire manufacturing surprisingly accelerating. Two positioning calls flip today. First, Canada goes to +2 and joins the euro at the top on the CPI rebound plus the best labour market in the G10. Second - and this is a correction to this book - the Swiss franc is NOT catching a haven bid: Trading Economics has it at a nearly one-year low with the SNB intervening specifically to limit safe-haven inflows and prevent excessive appreciation, so CHF drops to -1 and every franc-short cross is upgraded rather than sized down.

dailyRead: Two calls flip today and both come from the same source, so start there. Crude has now risen for a THIRD consecutive session: WTI is 85.37, up 1.03%, and Brent is 91.51, up 0.81% and the highest of the entire conflict. The proximate cause is a single sentence - President Trump said he is NOT interested in extending the interim peace deal, the 60-day memorandum of understanding signed in June that formally expired on Monday. Underneath it, three physical facts are doing the work. Washington will not support any Iran-Oman corridor arrangement that fails to guarantee unrestricted passage through the strait, and the US is not a party to those talks. Shipping through Hormuz collapsed over the weekend after attacks on tankers - only five commodity vessels transited on Saturday and NONE on Sunday, against 31 the previous weekend. And the EIA does not expect Middle East production back near pre-conflict levels until early 2027. What still caps the price rather than resolving it is that Gulf producers are becoming increasingly adept at moving barrels covertly with transponders off and supplying cargoes from outside the chokepoint. USOIL therefore goes UP to HIGH conviction. The first flip is Canada, and it is the most important data point on the page because it is the first hard evidence anywhere that the energy shock has reached core inflation. July CPI REBOUNDED to 3.0% from 2.8%, at the very ceiling of the Bank of Canada's 1-3% control range, driven by gasoline inflation accelerating to 25.7% from 20.5%. Crucially, the core measures did not hold - every single one ticked UP: CPI-median to 2.0% from 1.9%, CPI-trim to 1.9% from 1.8%, CPI-common to 2.7% from 2.6%, and core ex-food-and-energy to 2.3% from 2.1%, with services inflation up to 2.5% from 2.2%. Travel tours added 15.2% on World Cup demand. Only food at 3.0% from 3.5% and shelter at 1.3% from 1.5% eased. Set that against July employment of +75,100, the largest in two years, unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%, participation 65.1%, Canadian yields rising on strong macro data, and a policy rate at 2.25% sitting near the LOWER end of the Bank's estimated neutral range. CAD moves to +2 and joins the euro at the top of the ranking. The second flip is the Swiss franc, and it is a correction to what this book said yesterday. I wrote that the haven bid was becoming live as the ceasefire expired. It did not happen, and Trading Economics is explicit about why: the franc is at a NEARLY ONE-YEAR LOW against the dollar, and SNB foreign exchange intervention is supporting exporters by limiting safe-haven flows into the franc and preventing excessive appreciation. The domestic numbers are a funding currency's numbers and getting more so - July CPI 0.4%, a four-month low, core 0.3%, producer and import prices falling again at -2.1% y/y, unemployment 3.0%. The SNB is expected to hold at 0% through 2027 with cuts a contingency rather than a base case; most economists see the first hike in early 2028 and markets price one no earlier than March 2027. Even the Q2 GDP shock at +1.5% q/q points, in TE's reading, to LIMITED pass-through from higher energy prices. CHF drops to -1 WEAKENING and every franc-short cross is UPGRADED rather than sized down: EUR/CHF and CAD/CHF go to HIGH, AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF to MEDIUM. USD/CHF, which was a MEDIUM short, becomes RANGE because both legs are now weak. The dollar side of the book has stopped working and needs trimming rather than adding. The dollar index is 99.65 and HIGHER today, the first session in a week it has not made a low, with EUR/USD at 1.15727 down 0.07%, GBP/USD 1.35378 down 0.05%, AUD/USD 0.70975 down 0.11% and NZD/USD 0.58799 down 0.37% and the day's worst G10 performer. The US 10-year is 4.744% and rising, NY Empire manufacturing surprisingly accelerated, and June TIC inflows were 133.5 billion dollars. None of this undoes the four-print deterioration - payrolls CONTRACTING 23,000 with 146,000 of downward revisions, CPI 3.4% and core 2.5%, PPI 4.7%, retail sales -0.6% with the control group at -0.4% - and September is still around 67% for a hold. But Jackson Hole is nine days away on August 27, and a Chair looking for a reason to keep a hike alive now has crude at 85 and Brent at 91.5 to point at. USD moves from -2 to -1: still WEAKENING, but the unambiguous part is over. EUR/USD comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM and DXY from MEDIUM to LOW-MED. Tomorrow's FOMC minutes cover the July 29 meeting where Logan, Hammack and Kashkari dissented FOR a hike, and they predate every soft print, so the market will likely look through them. The euro keeps the top score at +2 and its case is unchanged and self-supporting: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% and services 3.3%, energy HICP accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, Q2 GDP confirmed at +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% against the 2.40% refi headline and the 2.65% marginal lending rate, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%. TE's own coverage says a September move is now almost fully priced and unless energy prices ease materially that view is unlikely to change - and with Brent at 91.5 they are not easing. Lagarde's second-round-effects justification has never looked better supported. Thursday brings the ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts, which will show how the wait-and-see language was actually agreed. The standing caution stands: consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5% and producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y. Australia comes DOWN to +1 and the reason is specific rather than mood. Consumer inflation expectations collapsed to 4.7% in July from 5.5%, quarterly GDP slowed to 0.3% from 0.9%, wage growth eased to 3.3% from 3.4%, business confidence is -6, job vacancies fell to 330,000 from 338,000, and the terms of trade dropped to 112 from 117. The hawkish frame is intact - cash rate 4.35% is the G10's highest, Bullock confirmed the Board discussed only hike-or-hold, the SoMP has underlying inflation at 3.3% into end-2026 with risks skewed UP, weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% and services to 4.0%, and the 10-year just broke above 5.0% - but a currency whose inflation expectations fall 80 basis points in a month while copper retreats 0.72% and global equities sell off does not deserve to sit alongside the euro. Thursday's July labour report at 01:30Z, consensus +20-25k after +76,343, is the decider. New Zealand gets a genuine correction UP, from -2 to -1. Yesterday this book said the July hike to 2.50% was the end of the cycle. Trading Economics says otherwise and TE is canonical: the kiwi is supported by expectations that the RBNZ will deliver ANOTHER quarter-point increase next month after repeatedly stressing the need to withdraw policy support, and the central bank is widely expected to raise again in September. That does not make the data good - unemployment at 5.6% is the highest since 2015, wage growth is 2.1%, two-year inflation expectations fell to 2.34% against a 2.7% forecast, the manufacturing PMI dropped hard to 54.3 from 60.1 with a majority of business comments turning negative, ANZ commodity prices decelerated to +0.5% and the GDT rose only 0.1% - but a central bank that is expected to hike cannot be scored -2. NZD/USD at 0.58799 was still the worst G10 performer today, down 0.37%, and rising crude directly worsens a terms-of-trade position where petrol already contributed 27.5% of headline CPI. The practical effect: EUR/NZD and AUD/NZD come DOWN from HIGH to MEDIUM, NZD/JPY and NZD/CHF go to RANGE, and the one kiwi short that gets BETTER is NZD/CAD, which goes to HIGH because the Canadian leg improved so much. Japan stays -1 MIXED and today made both sides sharper. USD/JPY firmed to 159.677, up 0.14% and within striking distance of the 160 level where the MoF has already acted, the Nikkei fell 2.20% to 67,698, and the 10-year JGB printed 2.936%, another multi-decade high, with roughly 62% still priced for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. Brent at 91.5 is unambiguously bad for Japan: the trade balance is already -407 billion yen, the current account swung to -923 billion from +3,968 billion, terms of trade have fallen to 81.62 and import prices are up 29.1% y/y with the index at a record 200. Against that, June industrial output was revised HIGHER to +1.9% m/m and +4.9% y/y, wages are 3.4% with real earnings positive for a sixth month, Tokyo CPI is 2.0% and Tokyo core 1.9%, PPI 7.2%, and inflation expectations 2.7%. Friday's July national CPI at 23:30Z Thursday, core expected 1.8% from 1.6%, decides September. Trade yen weakness through the crosses that also have an oil leg - CAD/JPY goes to HIGH and EUR/JPY to HIGH - not through USD/JPY, which stays a LOW-conviction short only on the policy tail. Sterling holds +1 with everything hanging on two prints. Q2 GDP was +0.4% q/q with the y/y rate at 1.2%, but the quarterly rate DECELERATED from 0.6%, unemployment is 4.9%, wage growth eased to 4.3% from 4.4%, the claimant count rose 6,700 from 1,300, and the July 30 decision was a 6-3 hold. The labour report lands at 06:00Z today and July CPI at 06:00Z tomorrow, where the headline will likely RISE mechanically on the Ofgem cap adjustment - a hawkish-looking print that is not really hawkish. Read core and services, not the headline. Finally the metals and the DAX, which all moved the same way and against the geopolitical narrative. Gold fell 0.68% to 4,386, silver 1.41% to 64.84 and copper 0.72% to 6.56 on profit-taking, in what TE called a broad metals retreat - on the day crude hit its conflict high. That is a market telling you the haven trade is crowded and the dollar has stopped falling. XAU comes DOWN from HIGH to MEDIUM, XAG to LOW-MED, XCU to RANGE. GER40 FLIPS from LONG to SHORT at LOW-MED: the DAX is 26,242 and down 0.37%, and it now faces rising energy input costs at Brent 91.5, an ECB that TE says is almost fully priced to hike on September 10, and a geopolitical risk-off bid all at once - three headwinds where a month ago it had a cheap-energy tailwind.

USD.when: Sept 16 FOMC (hold ~67% priced - but oil is re-arming the hawks)
USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike - Logan, Hammack and Kashkari - and Chair Warsh again declined to offer forward guidance. Re-verified on TE this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% from 3.5%, core 2.5% from 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000 from +20,000, retail sales -0.6% m/m, core PCE 3.3% y/y. The four-print deterioration is intact and unchanged: payrolls contracted in July with the prior two months revised down a combined 146,000, PPI final demand came in at 4.7% against 5.0% expected, and the retail sales Control Group printed -0.4% against +0.3% expected. What changed TODAY is the other side. The dollar index is 99.65 and HIGHER for the first session in a week, the 10-year is 4.744% and rising, the NY Empire State manufacturing index surprisingly accelerated, June TIC inflows were 133.5 billion dollars, and above all crude is at 85.37 with Brent at 91.51 - the conflict's high. The Michigan sentiment collapse to 51.0 already cited Middle East-driven prices, so the shock is reaching household expectations, and Canada has just printed the first hard evidence of energy passing into core. Wednesday's FOMC minutes at 18:00Z cover a meeting held BEFORE CPI, PPI, payrolls and retail sales all landed soft, so the market will probably look through them. Jackson Hole on Aug 27 is the real event and it is now materially more dangerous for dollar shorts than it looked a week ago. USD moves from -2 to -1: still weakening on the data, but the free part of the trade is over. July core PCE lands Aug 26.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (TE: 'almost fully priced' and energy is not easing)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike - the first in three years - with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and re-verified on TE this morning. Use the 2.25% depo, not the 2.40% headline. The domestic case is unchanged and self-supporting: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% and services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP confirmed at +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI 52.0, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, ZEW 23.4 from 9.5. TE's own coverage is the key line today: a September move is now almost fully priced, and unless energy prices ease materially that view is unlikely to change - with Brent at 91.51 and rising for a third session, they are not easing. Euro-area energy HICP was already accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, and Lagarde's stated justification for continuing to tighten is that the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects. Canada's July CPI, where gasoline at +25.7% pushed every core measure higher, is the first hard confirmation that the mechanism works. The ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts land Thursday at 09:30Z and will show how the wait-and-see language was actually agreed after the July hold. The standing caution stands: TE characterises the post-July stance as explicit wait-and-see, euro-area consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y and June retail sales were -0.3% m/m. EUR/USD is 1.15727, down 0.07% and stalling below Friday's two-month high, which is why the pair comes down to MEDIUM even as the euro keeps its +2.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; two prints decide it this week)
GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus, verified on TE today, with TE's end-of-quarter model still at 4.00%. The headline picture is decent but the momentum is not: Q2 GDP was +0.4% q/q, beating the +0.3% consensus with the y/y rate accelerating to 1.2% from 0.9% - but the quarterly rate DECELERATED from 0.6%. Unemployment is 4.9% with 1.76 million unemployed, wage growth eased to 4.3% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change was +148,000 from +99,000, and the claimant count rose 6,700 after 1,300. June CPI was 2.6% headline with core also 2.6% and services at 3.6%. Newsquawk's read of the GDP detail is that the June breakdown was weaker than expected, the May series was revised DOWN, volatile pharmaceuticals drove the manufacturing strength, and on balance it favours the members who made dovish arguments at the last meeting rather than the three dissenters. The unresolved negatives are real: the June trade deficit widened to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn, the RICS house price balance is -30, vacancies are 712,000 and below pre-pandemic, and inactivity is rising. The 10-year gilt at 5.088% is the highest in the G10 and is doing more for sterling than the MPC is. Two decisive prints inside 30 hours: the labour report TODAY at 06:00Z, and July CPI Wednesday at 06:00Z where the headline will likely RISE mechanically on the Ofgem utility cap adjustment even as PMI price gauges pointed to cooling. Read core and services, not the headline. GBP/USD is 1.35378 on the dollar leg, not the sterling one, and comes down to LOW-MED accordingly.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (~62% priced - and rising crude makes the case worse, not better)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%, verified on TE. Monday's preliminary Q2 GDP missed clearly at 0.3% q/q against 0.5% and 1.1% annualised against 2.0%, with flat private consumption and contracting business investment - and the rate market refused to take it. The 10-year JGB is 2.936% today, another multi-decade high, and roughly 62% is still priced for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. Today's overlay is worse for the yen, not better: USD/JPY firmed to 159.677, up 0.14% and inside the zone where the MoF has already demonstrated it will act, while the Nikkei fell 2.20% to 67,698. Brent at 91.51 transmits directly into Japanese weakness - the trade balance is -JPY 407bn, the current account swung to -JPY 923bn from +3,968bn, terms of trade have deteriorated to 81.62 from 82.71, and the import price index printed a record 200 from 197 with import prices up 29.1% y/y. That is exactly the tension the July Summary of Opinions described, and it was the most hawkish document of this cycle: one member named Middle East developments, expanding AI-related demand and a weak yen as forces pushing inflation up; another said inflation risks are skewed sharply to the upside as higher oil costs feed through; another said the pace of hikes could EXCEED market expectations; another said the cost of delaying is not insignificant. The domestic case is the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings including bonuses +1.6% and positive for a sixth month, June CPI 1.7% with core 1.6% and core-core 1.7%, Tokyo July CPI 2.0% and Tokyo core 1.9%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%. June industrial output was revised HIGHER to +1.9% m/m and +4.9% y/y. Unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18. Thursday's national CPI at 23:30Z, core expected 1.8% from 1.6%, is the decider; the trade balance lands with it.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (hawkish hold at 4.35% - but the expectations leg cracked)
AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 in a UNANIMOUS decision, verified on TE today, and the press conference did more work than the statement: Governor Bullock revealed the Board did NOT discuss a cut at all - only whether to raise or hold - said it is thinking hard about when it might be appropriate to raise rates, and that another hike was possible. The August Statement on Monetary Policy has underlying inflation at 3.3% by end-2026 with no return to the midpoint until late 2027 and risks skewed UP, and TE's model carries 4.60%. The 10-year has now broken above 5.0% at 5.069%. What justifies the downgrade to +1 is a cluster of TE readings that all point the same way. Consumer inflation expectations COLLAPSED to 4.7% in July from 5.5% - an 80bp fall in a single month, and the expectations channel is precisely what the RBA said it was protecting. Quarterly GDP growth slowed to 0.3% from 0.9%. Wage growth eased to 3.3% from 3.4%. Business confidence is -6. Job vacancies fell to 330,000 from 338,000. The terms of trade dropped to 112 from 117. The current account deficit widened to a record -AUD 27.1bn. The hawkish evidence is still there - Q2 weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, trimmed mean 3.6%, employment +76,343, participation 67.0%, commodity prices +15.4% y/y, services PMI 53.6 and composite 53.2 - but a high-beta commodity currency loses its top-tier claim on a day copper falls 0.72%, the ASX drops 0.39% and global equities sell off. Thursday's July labour force survey at 01:30Z, consensus +20-25k after +76,343 with unemployment 4.4-4.5%, is now the single biggest domestic risk in the book.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (CORRECTION - TE says another 25bp is expected)
NZD.note: This is a correction to yesterday's file, and TE is canonical. The OCR was raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years. Yesterday this book called that the end of the cycle. Trading Economics says the opposite: the kiwi is supported by expectations that the Reserve Bank will deliver ANOTHER quarter-point rate increase next month after repeatedly stressing the need to withdraw some of its policy support, and the central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates again in September after signalling the need to make policy less accommodative. NZD therefore moves UP from -2 to -1. The data does not justify more than that. Q2 unemployment is 5.6% against 5.4% expected and the highest since Q3 2015, with 171,000 unemployed; wage growth is just 2.1% y/y; employment rose 0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7%; youth unemployment is 17.2%. The Q3 RBNZ survey missed badly - two-year business inflation expectations at 2.34% against a 2.7% forecast and 2.53% prior, the lowest since Q4 2025, with one-year expectations collapsing to 2.60% from 3.41%. The manufacturing PMI dropped hard to 54.3 in July from 60.1, with TE noting a majority of business comments turned negative; the services PMI is 50.6 and consumer confidence 80.4. CAD.when: Sept 2 (hold, but the hike camp just got its print)
CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, re-verified on TE, with the Bank noting the economy was adjusting to recent shocks and that energy-driven inflation pressures were EASING. The important part is that the core measures did not absorb it: CPI-median rose to 2.0% from 1.9%, CPI-trim to 1.9% from 1.8%, CPI-common to 2.7% from 2.6%, core ex food and energy to 2.3% from 2.1%, and services inflation to 2.5% from 2.2%. Travel tours added 15.2% from 6.8% on World Cup flight and accommodation demand. Only food at 3.0% from 3.5% and shelter at 1.3% from 1.5% eased. Month-on-month the CPI rose 0.5% after a 0.4% drop. Layer that on the best labour market in the G10: July employment +75,100, the largest gain in two years, full-time +38,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% against expectations of no change, participation rising to 65.1%. Wage growth is a soft 3.4% y/y, which keeps this a growth story rather than a wage-inflation one, and the 10-year rose to 3.722% on strong macro data. The policy rate at 2.25% sits near the LOWER end of the Bank's estimated neutral range, so further cuts would push policy into accommodative territory - the asymmetry runs toward tightening. USD/CAD is 1.38758 and the loonie has now gained for a third straight week. CAD moves to +2 and joins the euro at the top. June retail sales land Friday at 12:30Z; the next CPI is Sept 14, two weeks after the Sept 2 decision.

CHF.when: Sept 24 SNB (zero through 2027 - and the SNB is selling francs)

TE is explicit: the franc is hovering near $0.81 after weakening to a NEARLY ONE-YEAR LOW, and foreign exchange interventions have supported exporters by limiting safe-haven flows into the franc and preventing excessive appreciation. Yesterday this book said the haven bid was becoming live as the ceasefire expired. It did not arrive, and today USD/CHF is 0.81165, UP 0.10%, with the franc weakening further on the day crude hit its conflict high. The domestic numbers are a funding currency's numbers and getting more so: July CPI 0.4% from 0.5%, its lowest in four months, core 0.3%, harmonised 0.7%, producer and import prices deflating again at -2.1% y/y, unemployment steady at 3.0%, the 10-year at just 0.393%. The SNB is expected to hold at 0% through 2027, with further cuts a contingency rather than the base case; most economists see the first hike only in early 2028, while markets price one no earlier than March 2027. CHF drops to -1 WEAKENING and every franc-short cross is UPGRADED: EUR/CHF and CAD/CHF go to HIGH, AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF to MEDIUM. USD/CHF becomes RANGE because both legs are weak, and NZD/CHF and CHF/JPY go RANGE for the same reason. US trade policy remains the standing uncertainty.

geopolitics: The escalation is now priced in the physical market rather than the headlines, and that is the change. Crude has risen for a THIRD consecutive session - WTI 85.37 up 1.03%, Brent 91.51 up 0.81% - to the highest levels of the entire conflict. The trigger was President Trump saying he is NOT interested in extending the interim peace deal: the memorandum of understanding signed in June, which gave both sides 60 days to negotiate a longer-term agreement, formally expired on Monday and will not be renewed. Three physical facts sit underneath the headline. First, shipping through the strait effectively stopped over the weekend after attacks on tankers - only five commodity vessels transited on Saturday and NONE on Sunday, against 31 during the previous weekend. Second, Iran and Oman continue to negotiate a corridor arrangement, with agreed coordinates for an inbound northern lane in Iranian waters and an outbound southern lane in Omani waters plus a joint coordination centre, but the US is not a party to those talks and Washington is unlikely to back any deal that fails to guarantee unrestricted passage. Iran's foreign ministry has not moved: as long as the US naval blockade continues, the conditions for reopening do not exist. Third, the EIA does not expect Middle East production to return near pre-conflict levels until early 2027 and sees Brent averaging 87 dollars across 2026 - a forecast the market is now trading above. What continues to cap the price rather than resolve it is physical leakage: Gulf producers are becoming increasingly adept at moving oil covertly through Hormuz with transponders switched off while also supplying cargoes from outside the chokepoint. The FX read has five parts and two of them are corrections to yesterday. First and most important, Canada delivered the first hard evidence anywhere that the energy shock has reached core inflation: July CPI rebounded to 3.0% with gasoline at +25.7% y/y, and CPI-median, CPI-trim, CPI-common and core ex-food-and-energy ALL rose. That is the mechanism working, and it takes CAD to +2. Second, the euro's hawkish case is directly reinforced - euro-area energy HICP was already accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, TE now describes the Sept 10 hike as almost fully priced and says only a material easing in energy would change that, and energy is not easing. Third, Japan is the clearest loser: the import price index printed a record 200 with import prices up 29.1% y/y, the trade balance is -JPY 407bn, the current account swung to -JPY 923bn and terms of trade fell to 81.62 - rising crude transmits into Japanese inflation and Japanese weakness simultaneously. Fourth, and this is the correction, the Swiss franc is NOT the escalation hedge this book assumed. TE has it at a nearly one-year low with the SNB intervening explicitly to limit safe-haven flows and prevent excessive appreciation, and TE reads both the Q2 GDP acceleration and the four-month-low 0.4% CPI as evidence of LIMITED pass-through from geopolitically driven energy prices. The franc failed to bid on the day crude hit its conflict high - so CHF drops to -1 and every franc-short cross is upgraded. Fifth, the metals refused the haven role entirely: gold fell 0.68% to 4,386, silver 1.41% to 64.84 and copper 0.72% to 6.56 in a single broad retreat, while equities sold off hard - Nikkei -2.20%, US100 -1.00%, DE40 -0.37%. That combination, risk-off equities with lower metals and a firmer dollar, is what a market repricing an inflation shock looks like rather than a fear shock, and it is why GER40 flips from LONG to SHORT and why the dollar short needs trimming into Jackson Hole on Aug 27, where Chair Warsh now has an energy argument he did not have a week ago.
